products.description: Review Readers' Favorite 5 Stars Reviewed By Jack Magnus for Readers' Favorite Sarah Ann Kinnear's adventure book for children, Little Pearl's Reflection: The Light in the Window, is a lovely story about Little Pearl and her adventures while searching for her mother.  Kinnear's story reminded me of the children's classic fairy tales written by fantasy writer, George MacDonald, and this story was a most welcome and pleasant surprise for this long-time MacDonald fan. Bodil Sebrina Christensen's illustrations are lovely and bring the island home of Little Pearl and her family to life. Little Pearl's Reflection: The Light in the Window is a grand selection for story or bedtime; it's also a perfect pick for a more advanced young reader. It's most highly recommended.From the blog, Lilacs in Literature, written by children's author Wanda Luthman - July 25, 2018"Today, I want to introduce you to a wonderfully creative and gifted children's author that I had the privilege to meet at a book event recently,  Sarah Ann Kinnear.I talked to her about her inspiration and book concept and was blown away by her multi-faceted books from being beautifully illustrated by a woman in Denmark, to the fun adventure stories told in a series of books, to the puzzle piece that is included in each book that will ultimately be something a child can put together!!More than your money's worth is included in these wonderful books, plus the positive messages inside." About the Author Sarah Ann Kinnear, a teacher and principal for 35 years, has worked in the classroom and behind the scenes educating children and creating innovative curriculum that encourages independent thought and creative problem solving. She has always appreciated imaginative stories and learning activities that inspire children and teenagers to ask questions, think for themselves and become life-long learners. Inspired by her experiences as a mother and a teacher, Sarah wanted to write an interactive adventure series for young children who enjoy books, puzzles, and mysteries. Little Pearl's Reflection is filled with suspense and surprises, including talking animals, plants - and even a talking river. Sarah lives with her husband and dog Huey in Pensacola, Florida. Visit the author online: https: //littlepearlsreflection.org and on Facebook: https: //m.facebook.com/littlepearlsreflection

products.description: Review “ A love letter to music and artistic creativity more broadly . It’s beautiful and unapologetically queer, Black, and brown , rejecting the notion that it needs to be quieter or like more familiar comics in order to succeed.…This book is a testament to Prince and how his music affected the world ." ― AV CLUB “The book leaves you no choice other than to get sucked into the funkadelicness … The book invites a deeper understanding of music, craft, and of legendary musicians themselves, but also never at the expense of fun and excitement . Illidge and Hannibal Tabu and artist Meredith Laxton mix ’80s fashion and names almost forgotten with themes of grief, reconciliation and perseverance that remain as pertinent as ever. MPLS Sound is a worthwhile read , a story that’s equally empathic and appreciative for the way things were and why things have to change .” ― COMICS XF About the Author Hannibal Tabu is a son, brother, husband, uncle, father and friend. He lives in southern Los Angeles with his wife and two daughters. He's a professional writer, editor, project manager and web producer, working with companies as varied as AOL, Quicken.com, Toyota Motor Sales, Express.com, California Association of REALTORS, Kaiser Permanente, Disney Channel, eHobbies/NextPlanetOver.com and American Honda. He's worked for more than two decades as a journalist, being published in Vibe, The Source, Rap Pages, Black Enterprise, The Los Angeles Sentinel, and on MTV Online. Hannibal has been writing since he was eight (when he wrote a truly atrocious novel about a very petty pantheon of gods), and has seen his poetry published in The Drumming Between Us, Voices From Leimert Park, Drumvoices Review, (Sic) Vice Verse, MultiVerse and other journals and anthologies. Former editor-in-chief of the Los Angeles Herald-Dispatch group of newspapers, Hannibal is also the author of novels THE CROWN: ASCENSION and FARAWAY (both available on Amazon, Barnes & Noble & Smashwords) and the upcoming sci fi political thriller ROGUE NATION. He won the 2012 Top Cow Talent Hunt and has written for Image Comics, Wunderman Comics, Legends Press, Aspen Comics, Canon Comics, Stranger Comics, and New Paradigm Studios. Hannibal writes The Buy Pile, a weekly comics reviews column for Comic Book Resources (http://cbr.cc) and can be found online at http://hannibaltabu.com.Meredith Laxton is a freelance illustrator from the capital of North Carolina. She has long been inspired by the storytelling of comics and tabletop RPGs. Her background in multimedia design and animation has aided her art career in the indie gaming scene with companies like Puny Human Games and InXile entertainment. Nowadays, Meredith resides in Savannah, Georgia, where she received her M.F.A. in Sequential Art.Joseph Illidge is a publishing executive, editorial director, creative showrunner, writer, and public speaker. His career in the publishing and media industries includes groundbreaking work for DC Entertainment, Heavy Metal, Valiant Entertainment, and various companies dedicated to storytelling narratives and their creators. His media coverage includes The Hollywood Reporter, Entertainment Weekly, The Washington Post, The New York Times, CNN Money, BBC, and Publishers Weekly. Joseph has been a speaker at the San Diego Comic-Con, The Apollo Theater, Purdue University, John Jay College of Criminal Justice, Skidmore College, The School of Visual Arts, the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, The Center for Fiction, and The San Francisco Public Library. Joseph was the Keynote Speaker at the C3 Comic Creator Conference in Long Beach, CA.

products.title: Another World: Nineteenth-Century Illustrated Print Culture
products.description: Review “A rich work . . . [that] traces the history of popular illustration in the nineteenth-century.”—Deirdre D. Spencer, ARLIS/NA Reviews “A fine contribution . . . A deeply researched and thoughtful book.”—P. A. Stirton, Choice “One of the most important contributions of Another World is its successful edging of photography aside. Mainardi’s study of mass cultural visual forms in the nineteenth century is in fact among the ﬁrst to dethrone the photograph from its usual position of dominance in histories of visual culture in the modern transatlantic world, and that is an achievement of wide-ranging importance.”—S. Hollis Clayson, Journal of Modern History “Another World provides a new, insightful analysis of the developments of graphic expression and visual culture in the nineteenth century and uncovers a trove of visual and textual materials that is rarely, if ever, addressed in depth. The book thus makes a vital contribution to the study of nineteenth-century print culture.”—Ruth E. Iskin, Ben-Gurion University of the Negev About the Author Patricia Mainardi is professor emerita of art history at the Graduate Center of the City University of New York and Chevalier in France’s Order of Academic Palms. She has received the College Art Association’s Charles Rufus Morey Award and numerous fellowships, including from the National Endowment for the Humanities and the Institute for Advanced Study.

2. **Harley Quinn & the Birds of Prey: The Hunt for Harley** (graphic novel, $26.99, 4.8 rating)

dialogue.agent:
Here's the full breakdown on each book!

---

**1. *Strangers 0: Omens & Origins*** — **$29.95** ⭐ 5.0

This is a superhero collection (not so much romance, actually) that reveals the origin stories of the "Strangers" superhero team — seven stories about characters like the Bronze Gladiator, Tanka, Futura, and Starlock. A reviewer called it a "new/old super universe" and said the writers "clearly love classic comics and present that style with a modern twist."

---

**2. *Harley Quinn & the Birds of Prey: The Hunt for Harley*** — **$26.99** ⭐ 4.8

Harley Quinn returns to Gotham to steal the Joker's legendary loot, but every super-villain in the city is after her. The Birds of Prey (Black Canary, Huntress, Renee Montoya, Cassandra Cain) come to her defense. Reviews are mixed — two 5-star reviews praise the artwork and story, while two 3-star reviews criticize the thin plot and say it relies on potty humor and inside references from the creative team's past run. It's described as a fun but lightweight endcap to the Conner/Palmiotti era.

---

**3. *Hillbilly Volume 3*** — **$17.99** ⭐ 4.8

An Appalachian fantasy graphic novel by Eisner Award winner Eric Powell. The hero Rondel wields the Devil's Cleaver against evil forces in the hills. Described as "Conan meets Grimm's Fairy Tales" with a primitive, vivid art style. Reviews are positive — one 5-star reviewer called it a "painted portrait of the American spirit" that weaves short stories into an interconnected epic. A 3-star reviewer felt the plot was a bit unoriginal but still a pleasant read, noting it might be better appreciated if you've read the earlier volumes.

---

Given your budget of $15–$30, all three qualify. Which one sounds most appealing to you? I can share more details if needed!

top_reviews.title: Great Art, But Lackluster Ending to Conner/Palmiotti's Harley Quinn Run
top_reviews.text:
Last year, in 2020, DC/Warner Brothers released “Birds of Prey (and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn)”, continuing Margot Robbie’s onscreen portrayal of Mister J’s crazy ex-girlfriend. So with the release of the film, it makes sense to release some new material pertaining to the leadup to the films release. Since Harley Quinn has gone full rated-R as of late, what with foul-mouth animated series of hers, Birds of Prey being R-rated, and this year’s “The Suicide Squad” by James Gunn going R-rated, it makes sense that comics would follow up on Harley going the same direction with Black Label, DC’s out of continuity/Mature brand.

When the film came out last year, I know of two Harley/Birds of Prey type books came out to comics readers. One was “BIRDS OF PREY”, a prestige 1-shot issue by Brian Azzarello (which was pretty mediocre.) The other is what is being reviewed here, “HARLEY QUINN AND THE BIRDS OF PREY”, with the return of THE NEW 52 creative team of Amanda Conner and Jimmy Palmiotti, who wrote Harley’s solo series from 2013 to end of 2017/early 2018. With the return of this creative team to Harley, we get a return to madcap Harley shenanigans that is easily the endcap/epilogue to their entire run.

HARLEY QUINN AND THE BIRDS OF PREY collects the 4-issue prestige run. Harley is living life in Florida, having a recent couple spat with her BFF/lover Poison Ivy, things aren’t going too well in her personal life. Things go even worse as her apartment building gets burnt down and her friend, Tony, gets assaulted. The people who hurt Tony and burnt her building sent a message, and when you tick off Harley, you throw down the gauntlet. The same people work out of Gotham, so it means Harley is going back to her old stomping grounds to get revenge. But with Harley turning anti-hero these past few years in comics, she’s burnt a lot of bridges with the villain community, so when Harley is back in Gotham, you know her ex, The Joker, wants his vengeance as well. Oh, and the Birds of Prey show up to assist Harley for some reason! (more on that later)

So following up on the release of the film, you’d think this book would tie-in to the films premise and characters. I am here to say that is not the case. Yes, the characters here are included because of the film, but all the characters here are based on their comic book counterparts and not the films (thankfully). Black Canary is not African-American, Renee Montoya is not Rosie Perez, and Cassandra Cain is not some pickpocket, Harley fangirl like the film. So even though this book’s title and release coincide with the theatrical release of the film at the time, they are not in any way tied to it.

Overall, HQ&BOP is a return to hijinks, potty humor, euphemisms, and sexual puns aplenty from Harley herself under the Black Label dropping F-bombs from the likes of characters I never thought I would hear from certain characters mouths . The book is nothing but a series of shenanigans from one situation into another, with the various cast trying to catch up behind her trail of destruction. Not much time is spent on character moments, just the shifting plot of Harley ratting out all of Jokers safe houses and his various stolen goods (including all Batman’s rogues valuables). Additionally, Conner and Palmiotti treat this 4-issue series as a endcap/coda/epilogue to their entire run on the character because everyone, and I mean just about EVERYONE that appeared in their past work together (including a character back in Palmiotti and Justin Grey’s Power Girl run) make some appearance here that are way too many to name drop. It makes for a great feeling of things coming full circle for the creative team’s history that I always appreciate. Granted, for new readers, it won’t be anywhere near as emotional or interesting as they will miss many easter eggs because they won’t know who or what the characters are or their connections to the creative team. Like Redtool, an obvious parody of Marvel’s Deadpool, that was created under Conner and Palmiotti’s New 52 Harley work. New readers will be baffled at this weird character and his inclusion to what is happening, and there are plenty of others that appear in the same way. But for those who have been with the creative team since then, it is a small joy in seeing those callbacks.

Wife and co-writer Amanda Conner rarely wrote comics because she is famous as an illustrator, so she only drew covers for the series. But here, we get Conner’s amazing artwork in oversized format and it never disappoints. She draws so much little mannerisms in characters expressions from rolling their eyes, to just little things lying around in her backgrounds. Food wrappers, opened doors, and even things like rocks are aspects most artist don’t include in their artwork, but Conners draws just about everything in her stuff. The only setback I have about her artwork, and it’s it is only a personal squabble I have, is I feel that I feel there are moments I feel Conner’s art is a tad lackluster in the faces. But again, personal and small tick from me.

As for the real setbacks, not being the art department, but the writing. Conner/Palmiotti writing on Harley Quinn since The New 52 series is written the same now as it was then, in that it is for low-brow humor that include tons of sexual euphemisms, fourth-wall breaking, and zany wording for which I do find it fun I admit, but it’s not something I can read steadily. This type of writing style is something akin to many Deadpool writers as well, where it’s majority of the story with little to any substance, world building, or character building (special mention to Daniel Way’s Deadpool run being the very example of this). Conner and Palmiotti’s work on Harley during the New 52 did this as well, but there was a decent amount of furthering the characters development that can be cited as worthy a decent look on Harley, if you can scrounge around those issues. But, there are various mini series Conner and Palmiotti also wrote that are just fluff like HARLEY QUINN AND POWER GIRL, HARLEY INVADES COMIC-CON, HARLEY’S LITTLE BLACK BOOK, and HARLEY’S GANG OF HARLEY’S are just some examples dumb fun comics akin to HQ&BIP. Sadly, I feel it’s very similar to here in. I had only read each issue at a time because I could only take so much of this writing style. Again, there’s moments I smiled and had a slight chuckle, but in terms of actual character building, HQ&BOP is another tale of pure hijinks that is only skin deep.

I even think the creative team a little out of steam here in the over premise. The overall synapsis I gave is really just that in 4 oversized issues: People attack Harley, Harley goes to Gotham to get back at attackers, every villain in Gotham is after Harley, things come to a crashing conclusion. Seriously, in terms of plot and pacing, it’s really paper thin. 80% is just pure zaniness to cover up the lack of story or character development. Again, Conner/Palmioitti’s Harley Quinn run is supposed to be fun, but it’s still really hard to do when you cover up what little story with so much fluff. And you know how I mentioned the Birds of Prey as an after thought? They really are. Seriously, they barely add anything to the story. Besides Renee Montoya having a few scenes, I feel as if the book could have cut them out entirely and it would not have changed anything to the story. Their presence here truly feels tacked on for the film release. All of they show up with little rhyme or reason. The worst one being Black Canary. Huntress, Cassandra Cain, and Montoya simply pop up on the page within four pages for no reason, and Black Canary just shows up at the beginning of issue #2 like she’d been there the whole time. Seriously, the creative teams’ writing on this just is lackluster.

So HARLEY QUINN & THE BIRDS OF PREY is a decent end to the Amanda Conner and Jimmy Palmiottti’s long run on Harley Quinn with all the bass humor that while fun, doesn’t last long. It’s another book to DC’s Back Label in having phenomenal oversized artwork thanks to Conner, but it’s so badly written. Unless you are a hardcore Harley Quinn, or hardcore fan of the creative teams works on Harley, and or here for the artwork, I think it’s the weakest entry to the Conner and Palmiotti’s work on Mister J’s former girl Harley.

top_reviews.title: Insulting to fans
top_reviews.text:
2.5 rounded up because I liked the Art style a lot and it did have some decent moments.

So. This one was...odd for me as a reader.

I enjoyed the run prior with Harley being revamped to be all into Beaver jokes and eating a lot. That stayed consistent, if a little overmuch with the horny schtick, and I still really adore Harley and Ivy together.

The very ending part though of the additional Harley red, black, and white issue shows Harley not only breaking the fourth wall (which she has done before), but also the writers having her sort of insult the audience...it made me feel annoyed. Like I was having a decent time with it until that last panel. Why would they add something like that?

To the point where even though I literally just spent $25 on it to read and keep on my shelves, I sort of want to just get rid of it now because it left me with a gross feeling after reading it.

top_reviews.title: Sharp As The Devil's Cleaver
top_reviews.text: What begins as a series of self-contained short stories is woven into an interconnected epic worthy of the Arthurian legend. HillBilly reminds us that people are actively thinking, feeling and creating in all parts of the country. When we start to listen to each other’s stories, they become a part of our identity. When we read really good fiction, we are no longer ourselves, but the characters. And so it concludes–with humanity of every class, color and gender united against the seemingly insurmountable forces of darkness. It’s a painted portrait of the American spirit. Not perfect, but resilient.

top_reviews.title: A sort of Apocalyptic Grimm Fairy Tale
top_reviews.text:
I have seen the Hillbilly series of graphic novels by Eric Powell described as "Appalachian folk fantasy", "Conan the Barbarian meets Grimm's Fairy Tales" and "Apocalyptic American Gothic" ... as well as in a bunch of other intriguing and interesting ways.

Having finally sampled the series with Volume 3 I can't say that I disagree with any of those descriptions to any great extent. The artwork has a very primitive get vivid style that compliments the story quite nicely. There is almost no color and when there is it is very muted, almost unnoticeable.

The weak point in this particular case, at least for me, is that the story and the plot are not particularly original. It's the basic good vs evil in a battle of the ages type of thing. We've seen it in one form or another hundreds of times and this version doesn't really do all that much that other variations on the theme haven't done before.

I thought it was okay but nothing spectacular. Granted, it is part of an ongoing series so it could well be that there are nuances and "Easter eggs" that I missed out on from not being familiar with previous entries in the series. I would definitely take another look at the series: Either with previous volumes or future offerings.

All in all Hillbilly Volume 3 was something of a pleasant time waster... I would stop short of giving it a high recommendation but I wouldn't discourage anyone from reading it either.

***Special thanks to NetGalley, the publisher, and the author for providing me with a complimentary digital copy in exchange for an honest review.

top_reviews.title: Great Art, But Lackluster Ending to Conner/Palmiotti's Harley Quinn Run
top_reviews.text:
Last year, in 2020, DC/Warner Brothers released “Birds of Prey (and the Fantabulous Emancipation of One Harley Quinn)”, continuing Margot Robbie’s onscreen portrayal of Mister J’s crazy ex-girlfriend. So with the release of the film, it makes sense to release some new material pertaining to the leadup to the films release. Since Harley Quinn has gone full rated-R as of late, what with foul-mouth animated series of hers, Birds of Prey being R-rated, and this year’s “The Suicide Squad” by James Gunn going R-rated, it makes sense that comics would follow up on Harley going the same direction with Black Label, DC’s out of continuity/Mature brand.

When the film came out last year, I know of two Harley/Birds of Prey type books came out to comics readers. One was “BIRDS OF PREY”, a prestige 1-shot issue by Brian Azzarello (which was pretty mediocre.) The other is what is being reviewed here, “HARLEY QUINN AND THE BIRDS OF PREY”, with the return of THE NEW 52 creative team of Amanda Conner and Jimmy Palmiotti, who wrote Harley’s solo series from 2013 to end of 2017/early 2018. With the return of this creative team to Harley, we get a return to madcap Harley shenanigans that is easily the endcap/epilogue to their entire run.

HARLEY QUINN AND THE BIRDS OF PREY collects the 4-issue prestige run. Harley is living life in Florida, having a recent couple spat with her BFF/lover Poison Ivy, things aren’t going too well in her personal life. Things go even worse as her apartment building gets burnt down and her friend, Tony, gets assaulted. The people who hurt Tony and burnt her building sent a message, and when you tick off Harley, you throw down the gauntlet. The same people work out of Gotham, so it means Harley is going back to her old stomping grounds to get revenge. But with Harley turning anti-hero these past few years in comics, she’s burnt a lot of bridges with the villain community, so when Harley is back in Gotham, you know her ex, The Joker, wants his vengeance as well. Oh, and the Birds of Prey show up to assist Harley for some reason! (more on that later)

So following up on the release of the film, you’d think this book would tie-in to the films premise and characters. I am here to say that is not the case. Yes, the characters here are included because of the film, but all the characters here are based on their comic book counterparts and not the films (thankfully). Black Canary is not African-American, Renee Montoya is not Rosie Perez, and Cassandra Cain is not some pickpocket, Harley fangirl like the film. So even though this book’s title and release coincide with the theatrical release of the film at the time, they are not in any way tied to it.

Overall, HQ&BOP is a return to hijinks, potty humor, euphemisms, and sexual puns aplenty from Harley herself under the Black Label dropping F-bombs from the likes of characters I never thought I would hear from certain characters mouths . The book is nothing but a series of shenanigans from one situation into another, with the various cast trying to catch up behind her trail of destruction. Not much time is spent on character moments, just the shifting plot of Harley ratting out all of Jokers safe houses and his various stolen goods (including all Batman’s rogues valuables). Additionally, Conner and Palmiotti treat this 4-issue series as a endcap/coda/epilogue to their entire run on the character because everyone, and I mean just about EVERYONE that appeared in their past work together (including a character back in Palmiotti and Justin Grey’s Power Girl run) make some appearance here that are way too many to name drop. It makes for a great feeling of things coming full circle for the creative team’s history that I always appreciate. Granted, for new readers, it won’t be anywhere near as emotional or interesting as they will miss many easter eggs because they won’t know who or what the characters are or their connections to the creative team. Like Redtool, an obvious parody of Marvel’s Deadpool, that was created under Conner and Palmiotti’s New 52 Harley work. New readers will be baffled at this weird character and his inclusion to what is happening, and there are plenty of others that appear in the same way. But for those who have been with the creative team since then, it is a small joy in seeing those callbacks.

Wife and co-writer Amanda Conner rarely wrote comics because she is famous as an illustrator, so she only drew covers for the series. But here, we get Conner’s amazing artwork in oversized format and it never disappoints. She draws so much little mannerisms in characters expressions from rolling their eyes, to just little things lying around in her backgrounds. Food wrappers, opened doors, and even things like rocks are aspects most artist don’t include in their artwork, but Conners draws just about everything in her stuff. The only setback I have about her artwork, and it’s it is only a personal squabble I have, is I feel that I feel there are moments I feel Conner’s art is a tad lackluster in the faces. But again, personal and small tick from me.

As for the real setbacks, not being the art department, but the writing. Conner/Palmiotti writing on Harley Quinn since The New 52 series is written the same now as it was then, in that it is for low-brow humor that include tons of sexual euphemisms, fourth-wall breaking, and zany wording for which I do find it fun I admit, but it’s not something I can read steadily. This type of writing style is something akin to many Deadpool writers as well, where it’s majority of the story with little to any substance, world building, or character building (special mention to Daniel Way’s Deadpool run being the very example of this). Conner and Palmiotti’s work on Harley during the New 52 did this as well, but there was a decent amount of furthering the characters development that can be cited as worthy a decent look on Harley, if you can scrounge around those issues. But, there are various mini series Conner and Palmiotti also wrote that are just fluff like HARLEY QUINN AND POWER GIRL, HARLEY INVADES COMIC-CON, HARLEY’S LITTLE BLACK BOOK, and HARLEY’S GANG OF HARLEY’S are just some examples dumb fun comics akin to HQ&BIP. Sadly, I feel it’s very similar to here in. I had only read each issue at a time because I could only take so much of this writing style. Again, there’s moments I smiled and had a slight chuckle, but in terms of actual character building, HQ&BOP is another tale of pure hijinks that is only skin deep.

I even think the creative team a little out of steam here in the over premise. The overall synapsis I gave is really just that in 4 oversized issues: People attack Harley, Harley goes to Gotham to get back at attackers, every villain in Gotham is after Harley, things come to a crashing conclusion. Seriously, in terms of plot and pacing, it’s really paper thin. 80% is just pure zaniness to cover up the lack of story or character development. Again, Conner/Palmioitti’s Harley Quinn run is supposed to be fun, but it’s still really hard to do when you cover up what little story with so much fluff. And you know how I mentioned the Birds of Prey as an after thought? They really are. Seriously, they barely add anything to the story. Besides Renee Montoya having a few scenes, I feel as if the book could have cut them out entirely and it would not have changed anything to the story. Their presence here truly feels tacked on for the film release. All of they show up with little rhyme or reason. The worst one being Black Canary. Huntress, Cassandra Cain, and Montoya simply pop up on the page within four pages for no reason, and Black Canary just shows up at the beginning of issue #2 like she’d been there the whole time. Seriously, the creative teams’ writing on this just is lackluster.

So HARLEY QUINN & THE BIRDS OF PREY is a decent end to the Amanda Conner and Jimmy Palmiottti’s long run on Harley Quinn with all the bass humor that while fun, doesn’t last long. It’s another book to DC’s Back Label in having phenomenal oversized artwork thanks to Conner, but it’s so badly written. Unless you are a hardcore Harley Quinn, or hardcore fan of the creative teams works on Harley, and or here for the artwork, I think it’s the weakest entry to the Conner and Palmiotti’s work on Mister J’s former girl Harley.

top_reviews.title: Sharp As The Devil's Cleaver
top_reviews.text: What begins as a series of self-contained short stories is woven into an interconnected epic worthy of the Arthurian legend. HillBilly reminds us that people are actively thinking, feeling and creating in all parts of the country. When we start to listen to each other’s stories, they become a part of our identity. When we read really good fiction, we are no longer ourselves, but the characters. And so it concludes–with humanity of every class, color and gender united against the seemingly insurmountable forces of darkness. It’s a painted portrait of the American spirit. Not perfect, but resilient.

top_reviews.title: A sort of Apocalyptic Grimm Fairy Tale
top_reviews.text:
I have seen the Hillbilly series of graphic novels by Eric Powell described as "Appalachian folk fantasy", "Conan the Barbarian meets Grimm's Fairy Tales" and "Apocalyptic American Gothic" ... as well as in a bunch of other intriguing and interesting ways.

Having finally sampled the series with Volume 3 I can't say that I disagree with any of those descriptions to any great extent. The artwork has a very primitive get vivid style that compliments the story quite nicely. There is almost no color and when there is it is very muted, almost unnoticeable.

The weak point in this particular case, at least for me, is that the story and the plot are not particularly original. It's the basic good vs evil in a battle of the ages type of thing. We've seen it in one form or another hundreds of times and this version doesn't really do all that much that other variations on the theme haven't done before.

I thought it was okay but nothing spectacular. Granted, it is part of an ongoing series so it could well be that there are nuances and "Easter eggs" that I missed out on from not being familiar with previous entries in the series. I would definitely take another look at the series: Either with previous volumes or future offerings.

All in all Hillbilly Volume 3 was something of a pleasant time waster... I would stop short of giving it a high recommendation but I wouldn't discourage anyone from reading it either.
